title: The Second Virial Coefficient
lead: The virial equation of state writes a real gas's pressure as a power series in its density. Its second coefficient comes from the potential between a pair of molecules, worked out here for hard spheres, hard convex bodies and the van der Waals gas.
notes: Adapted from SklogWiki and Stefan Franzen, shared under CC BY 4.0 at the source and here under the book's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
exercise_notes: The section prints no exercises; both here are new and AI-written, their answers checked by computation, with Bloom levels and concept tags chosen by AI. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

exercises.source_id: For the hard sphere model one has:
exercises.prompt: Hard spheres of diameter $\sigma = 3.40$ Å have $B_2 = 2\pi\sigma^3/3$ per molecule. What is $B_2$ per mole, in cm³/mol? ($N_0 = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$ mol⁻¹)

answer.hint: Work in centimeters, 1 Å = 10⁻⁸ cm, and multiply by Avogadro's number.
answer.solution: Per molecule, $B_2 = 2\pi(3.40 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{cm})^3/3 = 8.23 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3$. Per mole it is $N_0$ times that, $(6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1})(8.23 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3) = 49.6\ \text{cm}^3/\text{mol}$, at every temperature.

exercises.source_id: For the Van der Waals equation of state one has:
exercises.prompt: For N₂, $a = 1.43$ L² bar mol⁻² and $b = 0.03913$ L/mol (Table 16.2.1). Find $B_2 = b - a/RT$ at 300 K in cm³/mol, with $R = 0.08314$ L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Which wins at this temperature, the excluded volume or the attraction?

answer.hint: Work out a/RT in L/mol first, then convert to cm³/mol.
answer.solution: $a/RT = 1.43 / (0.08314 \times 300) = 0.0573$ L/mol $= 57.3$ cm³/mol, and $b = 39.1$ cm³/mol, so $B_2 = 39.1 - 57.3 = -18.2$ cm³/mol. The negative sign means the attraction outweighs the excluded volume at 300 K; $B_2$ turns positive only above $T = a/Rb = 440$ K.

footnotes.html: The ideal term is $P/\rho kT$, with $\rho$ the number density; the virial coefficients give most of its departure from 1.
Here $\sigma$ is the diameter of the hard sphere, the distance between the centers of two spheres in contact. The integral up to $\sigma$ and the result $2\pi\sigma^3/3$ both need that distance.
